description:
We are Team Tanyl from Shymkent, Kazakhstan, now joined with team SARWatch for the global round.

We build FireCalendar: NASA MODIS and VIIRS fire data harmonized into one 25-year record, machine-learning fire-risk forecasts, NISAR radar burned-area checks, AI after-fire reports and alerts in Kazakh, Russian and English. Skills: Python, machine learning, remote sensing, web development, design.

Looking for: GIS and radar specialists, emergency-service experts, translators.
summary:
FireCalendar answers one question for Central Asia and the USA: is this a normal fire season? 
NASA's two fire sensors disagree: VIIRS (375 m, since 2012) sees about three times more hotspots than MODIS (1 km, since 2000), so joining the raw records creates a false jump in 2012. We convert MODIS into VIIRS units with a transparent model (month ratio, local 25 km factor, small-fire fill), validated on unseen years: R² 0.991, bias +0.8%. The resulting 25-year record shows fire activity in Central Asia falling about 60% per decade (p < 0.0001), a trend VIIRS alone cannot prove.

On this record we trained machine-learning forecasts of unusual fire activity 14 days ahead per province (AUC 0.81 vs 0.63 for the seasonal baseline) and per 25 km place, explained by AI briefings with concrete actions, plus browser and Telegram fire alerts.

New in this update, merged with team SARWatch: after-fire reports for journalists and emergency services. They express each fire in burned km² from three satellites (VIIRS, MODIS MCD64A1, NISAR radar) and add what burned, nearby settlements, the weather, and an AI write-up in Kazakh, Russian and English.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
FireCalendar is a free web app for residents, regional emergency services, journalists and analysts in five Central Asian countries (Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan) and in the United States. Pick a country, province, point or rectangle and a month: the app tells you whether fire activity is normal, shows 25 years of history, the fire season, the trend, and a 14-day forecast.

HOW WE HARMONIZED MODIS AND VIIRS (the challenge)
VIIRS (375 m) detects small fires that MODIS (1 km) misses, so raw counts jump about 3x in 2012 although nothing changed on the ground. On a 0.25° grid by month, using the years when both sensors fly (2012-2021), we estimate:
- a VIIRS/MODIS ratio for each calendar month (seasonality of small fires),
- a local multiplier for each 25 km cell, shrunk toward 1 where data are sparse,
- the expected VIIRS-only small fires where MODIS saw nothing,
- a Terra-only correction for 2000-2002.
Every MODIS hotspot gets a weight in VIIRS units; since 2012 we use VIIRS directly. Any area is the sum of weights, with a 90% uncertainty band. Trained on 2012-2018 and tested on unseen 2019-2021: R² 0.991 on log monthly totals, bias +0.8%. Result: 2001-2025 activity in Central Asia falls about 60% per decade (Mann-Kendall p < 0.0001); VIIRS alone (2013+) gives p = 0.10.

AI AND MACHINE LEARNING
- 14-day forecast per province (gradient boosting, 18 inputs: NASA POWER heat, dryness, rain, soil moisture, wind, plus current fires, neighbours and season). Trained 2001-2018, tested 2019-2025: AUC 0.814 vs 0.628 for the seasonal baseline. The "Why" panel shows the drivers.
- Forecast for every 25 km place (AUC 0.841 vs 0.835 baseline; small gain, stated honestly, useful for where to look inside a province).
- Claude (Anthropic) explains the numbers: an AI briefing for emergency services with who / what / when actions, and a chat assistant that answers only from our own API.

NEW IN THIS UPDATE: AFTER-FIRE REPORTS (joint work with team SARWatch)
For the largest fires the app builds a fact sheet:
- how the fire grew day by day (VIIRS detections);
- burned area in one unit, km², from three satellites: the VIIRS fire footprint, NASA MODIS MCD64A1 burned-area maps (500 m), and NASA NISAR L-band radar before/after comparison computed with SARWatch (sees through smoke and clouds). A calibration over many fires converts any fire's footprint into expected burned km² with a range;
- what burned (ESA WorldCover 10 m);
- settlements within 15 km with distance and population, and roads and power lines crossing the area (OpenStreetMap);
- weather during the fire vs the usual (NASA POWER) and the fire's size rank in its province since 2012;
- an AI write-up in Kazakh, Russian or English: a news summary for journalists and an after-action note with lessons and next-season actions for emergency services, using only the facts on the page;
- one-click print / PDF.
We report radar results honestly: with passes six to eight weeks apart, NISAR separates the burned area only weakly in US forests and not on Kazakh grassland. We show this as a measured limit and a next step.

ALERTS
Browser push alerts (no app, any country) and a Telegram bot (@NasaTanylBot) warn when satellites detect a new fire within a chosen radius.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT
- Emergency services get a ranked, explained 14-day risk and after-action reports.
- Journalists get verified numbers, maps and sources in their language.
- Residents get plain answers and alerts.
A civil protection officer in Shymkent reviewed the app and valued how quickly it lets him monitor and analyze the situation.

TOOLS
Python, FastAPI, DuckDB, pandas, scikit-learn, shapely, rasterio; JavaScript, Leaflet, ECharts; Vercel (serverless + private Blob storage); Web Push; Claude API. SARWatch: FastAPI, React, rasterio, h5py, Docker on Render. Three languages: Kazakh, Russian, English.


CREATIVITY AND CHOICES
Transparent harmonization instead of a black box, so every coefficient can be explained. Honest validation on unseen years, including where a model adds little. One site per region from a single code base. Designed with emergency-service feedback; every block folds so the map stays readable on phones.

Live sites: https://fire-calendar.vercel.app (Central Asia), https://fire-calendar-usa.vercel.app (USA)
Code: https://github.com/anirecake/Fire-calendar
